title: What does one order leave you?
principle: Price minus stock cost isn't profit. Count every hidden cost.

screens.text: Let me start with a story. In 2015, an app called PepperTap promised your groceries at home in two hours. By October it handled 20,000 orders a day in 17 cities, and investors had put in more than $50 million. Before I tell you what happened next, have a guess.

screens.prompt: In April 2016, PepperTap shut its grocery delivery. What do you think went wrong?

options.label: A bigger rival took its buyers

screens.why: It was each order. People did order, thousands of times a day, but the founder later wrote that the cash burnt on every single order kept rising. So every new order made the loss bigger, not smaller.

screens.title: The costs that ride along
screens.text: Now you know what happened, but how can an order lose money when the customer pays for every packet? The groceries were only one cost. Every order also carried a discount and a rider's trip, so let's look at what one order really left behind.

screens.title: What one order leaves
screens.text: Think of each order as a bucket of water you carry home. The price fills it, and every cost that order brings, like stock, delivery, a discount or packing, is a hole. What reaches home is called the contribution margin, and rent and salaries still come out of it.

screens.prompt: Let's try one. An app sells ₹500 of groceries and keeps ₹80 after paying the shop. Delivery costs ₹50, the discount ₹40. What's left?
screens.why: Exactly. ₹80 minus ₹50 for delivery and ₹40 for the discount leaves −₹10, so this order loses ₹10. A ₹500 bill looks healthy, but the contribution margin tells you the truth.

wrong.a: I see what you did: ₹80 is what's left after the shop is paid. But delivery and the discount come out of that same ₹80, and together they cost ₹90, so the order loses ₹10.
wrong.b: You took off delivery, and ₹80 − ₹50 is ₹30. The ₹40 discount comes out of that too, which leaves −₹10, a loss.

screens.prompt: So if every order loses ₹10, what happens when the app doubles its orders?

options.label: The loss shrinks, because the app is bigger

screens.why: Right. At ₹10 lost per order, 20,000 orders lose ₹2 lakh a day, and 40,000 orders lose ₹4 lakh. Growing a losing order only grows the loss, so before you chase more orders, make sure each one leaves something behind.

wrong.a: I see why you'd think that, because big businesses often get cheaper costs. But here each order still loses ₹10, so twice the orders means twice the loss.
wrong.c: Nothing changes for a single order: it still loses ₹10. More orders just add up more losses, so the loss doubles.

screens.title: Now it's your business
screens.text: Let's see if you can spot the holes yourself. Imagine you sell your own T-shirts on Instagram at ₹499 each. A shirt costs you ₹180 to make, so it looks like you keep ₹319 an order. Before you believe that, think about what else every order costs you.

screens.prompt: Each order also costs ₹70 shipping, ₹15 packing, a ₹10 payment fee and ₹150 in ads. What's your real contribution margin?
screens.why: Well done. ₹319 minus ₹70, ₹15, ₹10 and ₹150 leaves ₹74. Notice that the ads alone ate almost half of what you thought you kept, and you'd never see that on the price tag.

wrong.a: I see what you did: you took off shipping, packing and the fee. But you also paid ₹150 in ads to find this buyer, so that comes off too, and you're left with ₹74.
wrong.c: That's price minus the shirt, which is where most sellers stop. But every order also brings shipping, packing, a fee and ads, and after those you keep ₹74.

screens.prompt: One in five cash-on-delivery buyers refuses the parcel. It earns nothing but costs ₹305 in ads, packing and two-way shipping. What do five orders leave?
screens.why: That's it. The four delivered orders leave 4 × ₹74 = ₹296, but the refused one cost ₹305, so together the five leave −₹9. A sale that looks good on its own can turn into a loss once failed orders count, which is why so many sellers ask buyers to pay first.

wrong.b: You counted the four delivered orders correctly: they leave ₹296. But the refused parcel didn't just earn nothing; it cost ₹305, so the five orders together leave −₹9.
wrong.c: I see what you did: 5 × ₹74. But only four orders were delivered, and they leave ₹296, while the refused parcel cost ₹305. Together, that's −₹9.

screens.prompt: Back to a prepaid order. If you could cut one cost by 20%, which cut saves you the most?
screens.why: Exactly. 20% of the ₹180 shirt is ₹36, against ₹30 off the ads and ₹14 off shipping. Most sellers fight with the courier first, but a better deal from your maker is worth more.

wrong.b: Close, because ads are a big cost. But 20% of ₹150 is ₹30, while 20% of the ₹180 shirt is ₹36.
wrong.c: The courier is the first cost most people try to cut, but 20% of ₹70 is only ₹14. Go for the biggest cost: 20% of the ₹180 shirt saves ₹36.

screens.prompt: Your plain shirt leaves ₹74 and sells 15 a week. A printed one leaves ₹130 and sells 10. Which earns you more each week?

options.label: The plain one, because it sells more

screens.why: Well done. The plain shirt earns 15 × ₹74 = ₹1,110 a week, while the printed one earns 10 × ₹130 = ₹1,300. A fast seller can earn less than a slow one, so count rupees per week, not shirts.

wrong.a: I see why: more shirts feels like more money. But 15 × ₹74 is ₹1,110, while 10 × ₹130 is ₹1,300, so the slower shirt earns more.
wrong.b: Work out each one: 15 × ₹74 = ₹1,110 and 10 × ₹130 = ₹1,300. The printed shirt earns ₹190 more a week.

screens.setup: Then a shop owner from Surat calls. She wants 100 of your shirts a month at ₹350 each. She'll collect them herself, so there's no shipping, no ads and no refused parcels, and you'd only pack them, at ₹15 a shirt.
screens.question: ₹350 is far below your ₹499 price. What do you do?

options.label: Say no. I'd lose ₹149 a shirt
options.outcome: She buys from another maker. You keep selling online at ₹499, where a good order leaves you ₹74, and the ₹15,500 a month her order would have left you goes to someone else.
options.why: You compared prices, not what each sale leaves. ₹350 − ₹180 − ₹15 = ₹155, which is double what a ₹499 online order leaves you.
options.better: Work out what each shirt leaves before you say no.

options.label: Work out what each shirt leaves, then decide
options.outcome: ₹350 minus the ₹180 shirt and ₹15 packing leaves ₹155 a shirt, more than double the ₹74 an online order leaves. You say yes, and 100 shirts leave you ₹15,500 a month.
options.why: Well played. A lower price with fewer holes in the bucket can leave you more than a high price with many.

options.label: Say yes only if she pays ₹499
options.outcome: She says no and stops replying. A week later you agree to ₹350 after all, but she has already given half the order to another maker, so 50 shirts leave you ₹7,750 a month.
options.why: You pushed on the price when the margin was already good, and that cost you half the order.
options.better: Count the margin first, so you know when a price is already good.

screens.text: Price minus stock isn't profit. What one ___ leaves after every cost it causes is its contribution ___.
screens.why: Exactly. PepperTap had 20,000 orders a day, but more orders can't rescue an order that loses money. What each sale leaves is what pays your rent and wages, so before you chase more sales, I want you to check that one sale leaves you something.

summary: Contribution margin is what one order leaves after every cost it causes.
Ads, delivery, discounts and refused parcels can turn a 'good' sale into a loss.
A fast seller can earn less than a slow one. Count rupees per week.

cards.front: Price ₹600, stock ₹300, delivery ₹80, ads ₹200. What's the contribution margin per order?
cards.back: ₹600 − ₹300 − ₹80 − ₹200 = ₹20. Every cost an order causes comes off.

cards.front: Item A leaves ₹5 and sells 100 a day. Item B leaves ₹12 and sells 50. Which earns more a day?
cards.back: B: ₹600 a day. A: ₹500. Count rupees, not units.
